title: Children aged 5, 8 and 11 killed in US school shooting before suspect shot by bystander
content: A 16-year-old has shot dead three children and a teacher at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander, police said. The suspect, who has not been named, forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz confirmed. The teenager was shot dead by a community member who "pursued him into the school and engaged him", Krantz said. Police arrived three minutes later. The three children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a hospital in a critical condition. It is unclear if the attacker had any links to the school. "We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Steven Cook, the top administrative official of the local school district, said in a statement. "No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing." Police said the attacker was a local 16-year-old boy, but they did not release any further details on him or the identity of the victims. Police were alerted to an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary at 12:59 local time (19:59 GMT), Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters. The first call came from a person who said that an unknown suspect was shooting into their car with a long gun, police said. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes. Minutes later, the local county dispatch received 911 calls reporting that the attacker had entered the school. Police said he shot at locks on the doors in order to force his way inside. Local media reports suggested the school received new classroom doors in 2022 which can be locked with the flip of a switch. A bystander saw the shooting begin to unfold, pursued the attacker into the school and shot him dead, police explained. Three minutes later, officers first arrived at the scene. They confirmed that the attacker had been killed, and then searched the school. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised the bystander who "heroically intervened" to stop further loss of life. "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she told a media briefing alongside other officials. A local newspaper reporter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the school was in lockdown during the shooting and that students were able to communicate with parents outside with their Apple watches. Michael Kohn, a reporter with Bulletin newspaper, said the incident had left the parents stunned. "This is a neighbourhood school. Parents are stunned. It's just something you don't expect to happen in Bend, Oregon. It's a mountain town," he said. Schools in Bend have been closed on Friday. Officials said the community needed time to heal. Around 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary School, which has more than 40 adult staff members, police said. According to the K-12 School Shooting Database, there were 235 shooting incidents at American schools last year and at least 140 so far this year. Gun control advocacy group Everytown for Gun Safety has ranked Oregon 12th in the list of US states on the strength of its gun laws. But gun violence rate in the state is near the national average at 14.2 deaths per 100,000 residents, according to the group. Jay Jhaver believes he is the only West Bromwich Albion fan in Arizona, USA. The BBC's Sarah Smith travelled across the state ahead of the midterms, as the president faces political headwinds. Edward "Buddy" Jackson's body was found stuffed in a barrel in 2022, with a gunshot wound to the head. Police say he likely was killed four decades ago. The alleged plot only failed because the 19-year-old suspect's gun jammed outside the place of worship, say police. A number of states have confirmed they were targeted by the mailings, including Oklahoma, Ohio and Louisiana. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: At the scene of a school roof collapse in Pakistan
content: A school roof has collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar. At least 33 pupils and a teacher were killed according to hospital officials, and more than a dozen were injured. Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes". The BBC's Carrie Davis reports from the scene. Thick orange smog descended on the Indonesian city of Palangka Raya as wildfires continue raging nearby. Châtaigniers en fleurs, also known as Chestnut Trees in Blossom, is expected to receive record bids at auction this weekend. The critically endangered apes were rescued from intense wildfires that destroyed their habitat in August and September. A flash flood at the Budhi Gandaki River has swept away several buildings and bridges, two months after catastrophic floods hit the country. Tens of thousands of security personnel have been deployed and roads barricaded in Delhi to stop the latest Cockroach Janta Party demonstration. Thailand’s Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household. The BBC’s Tessa Wong breaks down how one of Indonesia’s worst wildfire seasons is impacting countries around South East Asia. Indonesian lawmakers on Wednesday ordered the demolition of a controversial luxury compound inside a penitentiary near the capital. The municipality building in Baglung was left teetering on an unstable ledge due to floods before it fell into a river. Days of near continuous downpours have caused widespread flooding in the Thai capital. The BBC is in Inner Mongolia where dozen of Chinese data centres are being constructed, as the country aims to lead the world in artificial intelligence. Lian Yunzhi broke the women's world record twice in three days at World Cube Association competitions. Verified footage appears to show a cargo ship colliding with a fishing boat near Singapore, with investigators still working to establish exactly when and how the crash happened. The BBC goes inside a fortified storage facility to view luxury goods seized by police that are now up for auction. Rescuers are searching for survivors after the vessel travelling from the mainland to a popular tourist destination caught fire. There are still hundreds of workers trapped in a network of tunnels that run along the Trishuli river. BBC South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri is in Nepal where authorities are trying to begin rebuilding amid the debris. Galaxy Robot Park is a 16,500-square-meter venue in South Korea, with attractions including humanoid robots dancing to K-pop hits. The BBC's Jonathan Head looks at the historical echoes of US troops arriving in Pattaya, a beach resort famous for its racy bars. The BBC's Tokyo correspondent Kurumi Mori tries Japan's latest food trend, instant noodles made using cold water. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: US intel officials postpone classified threat briefing for election officials after technical difficulties
content: US intelligence officials had to postpone a much-anticipated classified briefing for election officials about foreign threats because the video call was plagued by technical difficulties, according to six people familiar with the matter. Election officials from across the country, who rearranged their schedules on short notice less than three weeks before Election Day, were left frustrated after federal officials were unable to get the video call to work on Thursday, the sources said. The briefing was set to be the first time since the 2024 presidential election that state election officials heard from federal agencies in a classified setting about the threat environment from foreign powers like Russia, Iran and China, according to three of the sources. Officials from the FBI and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence planned to lead the briefing, while the Department of Homeland Security’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) was supposed to help facilitate it. “Glad they don’t run the election,” one person familiar with the call said, referring to the federal officials who organized the call. Invites to election officials went out just a couple days prior to the briefing, and some election officials who wanted to get access to the briefing were unable to, one of the sources familiar with the call said. One county election director said their security team wasn’t able to connect to the briefing due to the technical difficulties. An election official in another state said the briefing was “abruptly cancelled” about 15 to 30 minutes after it was scheduled to begin, and that the federal officials didn’t offer much explanation. CNN has requested comment from all three federal agencies that hosted the aborted briefing. The mishap comes as many Americans have already cast their ballots in the midterm elections, and as US intelligence officials continue to monitor for attempts by foreign powers such as Russia and Iran to sow discord among voters. At least one election official who spoke to CNN pointed out that the briefing was supposed to take place the same week that multiple election offices received suspicious letters containing white powders. That matter is now under investigation by the FBI, and the briefing Thursday was unrelated to the letters. The blunders in organizing Thursday’s briefing stem from the fact that federal officials in the second Trump administration have not been in touch as regularly with election officials about security issues as in prior administrations, three of the sources said. In the first Trump administration and the Biden administration after, the FBI, CISA and ODNI regularly briefed election officials on the latest intelligence on Russia, Iran and China’s possible intentions toward the midterm and general elections. The briefings covered hacking threats, disinformation and other activity emanating from those nations and from others. But the second Trump administration disbanded or downsized several government centers that were tasked with repelling foreign influence operations. The administration also dismantled CISA’s election security work and fired or reassigned many of the agency’s experts on the subject. In the last three months, the Trump administration has begun to rebuild some of that election security work while continuing to pursue evidence that supports the president’s false claims of widespread election fraud. In June, CISA told Congress that it had assigned new officials to build “trusted relationships” with state and local elected officials, CNN has reported . Last month, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed a memo directing the military to defend the US midterm elections from foreign interference. The activities outlined in the memo are largely things that US military and spy agencies were doing to protect American elections from foreign threats prior to Donald Trump returning to the presidency in 2025. Trump has also continued to dismiss or question past US intelligence about Russian and Chinese efforts to influence elections. Those factors prompted widespread concern among current and former US national security officials that the second Trump administration was not prioritizing defending US elections from foreign meddling.
